title: GPU admission control and co-residency
subtitle: Two models on one GPU, with the second admitting work against measured memory and refusing with a number: a 0.6B router beside a 30B model, through a 2,048-client burst.

stats.label: MiB, the router's whole footprint beside the resident model

lede: Capabilities model had to run on a Blackwell GPU whose memory belonged to a 30-billion-parameter model that stayed resident and serving. Agents call the discovery model before most actions, so many would call it at once, and a wrong answer under load would be worse than a slow one. I gave it a fixed memory budget and made two thousand concurrent clients an acceptance criterion from the start. The engine admits work against the memory it has measured, so overload becomes a queue and then a refusal and never a corrupted answer.
quote: I set the acceptance numbers before the engine exists so the result cannot be reframed afterwards.
evidence: GPU co-residency and admission control: a 0.6B router in 2,740 MiB beside a 30B serving model, admitting work against measured memory and refusing with the shortfall and a retry hint.
Load testing at concurrency: a ladder to 2,048 clients with abort conditions at every rung, the burst served at 85.9 requests per second with none failed, rejected or corrupted.
Honest performance reporting: mixed traffic reported at 6.9 requests per second against a pre-registered target of 200 rather than a flattering count of about 14.
High-throughput batch inference: admission in front of TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batcher with a minimum-batch token gate and backpressure counted at the GPU.
author: Corey James
